newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Samsung report renews Kia Motors takeover talk.
newsitem.headline: Samsung report renews Kia Motors takeover talk.

text.p: The powerful Samsung Group is testing the waters for a potential takeover of South Korea's second-largest carmaker by leaking an internal report recommending restructuring of the overcrowded industry, analysts said.

"By releasing its own information, Samsung is trying to check public and government opinion about its intention to take over Kia Motors," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.

The internal Samsung report, which came to light last week, proposed restructuring the domestic car industry to overcome a possible crisis in the sector following excessive investment in facilities and an unstable supply and demand situation.

Kia Motors Corp said Samsung also argued in the report that confidence in Kia's top managers had been lost and that Kia faced "internal managerial conflicts." It said the Samsung report said Kia had reached its maximum growth potential.

Angry Kia officials filed a complaint with prosecutors against Samsung Motor Inc on Saturday and said the company was considering filing a lawsuit this week for compensation for expected losses and damage to Kia's reputation.
"Our patience is exhausted," Kim Sun-hong, chairman of Kia Motors, told reporters.
A Samsung Motor spokesman acknowledged the existence of the internal report but said he could not comment.
Kim said: "Everybody will laugh as the latecomer, producing no cars yet, is trying to wield a restructuring sword."
"It's unethical activity. It's not worth commenting on," said Lee Jong-gyu, president of Ssangyong Motor.
An analyst who asked not to be named said the release of the Samsung report reflected Samsung's owns problems in car production.
Samsung has never admitted an intention to take over Kia but analysts said takeover rumours have repeatedly resurfaced since three Samsung affiliates acquired a total 9.6 percent stake in Kia 1993.
At that time, some analysts said a takeover would have been good for both Kia and Samsung, but Samsung backed down and reduced its holding in Kia to about six percent.
Samsung won government approval in 1994 to enter the cut-throat car industry in a technical tie-up with Japan's Nissan Motor Co despite strong opposition due to concerns of oversupply.

The analyst and local media said Samsung had failed to secure enough parts suppliers and faced funding problems, even though huge amounts of money were needed in the future in addition to two trillion won ($2.24 billion) already invested.
Samsung Electronics, a major money source for Samsung Motor, was no longer a cash cow due to a slump in the global semiconductor industry, analysts said.

"Samsung eventually targets to be a global carmaker. But it will take a long time and too much money to reach one million vehicle output capacity -- the minimum requirement to be globally competitive," Rhee said.
Samsung Motor plans to produce 80,000 vehicles in 1998, with annual production rising to 250,000 units in 1999 and 500,000 units in 2002.
Rhee of Dongbang Peregrine said Kia would be a good solution to Samsung's woes as it has good franchise and distribution networks and production facilities.
Kia has brought the issue to the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association, seeking collective action against Samsung Motor.
"We take the Samsung report very seriously. We will unveil our stance on Monday," the association's president Chung Mong-gyu told reporters.
(Conversion $1 = 891 won)
